query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles preserve their structural and chemical stability under high temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions primarily because the random, near-equiatomic mixing of multiple elements induces significant lattice distortion that reduces atomic diffusion, thereby suppressing phase separation and coalescence.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic, disordered solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized via methods that promote random elemental mixing (HEA-NPs).
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles with identical overall compositions: one set synthesized under conditions that yield a high-entropy, randomly mixed state, and a control set subjected to post-synthesis annealing designed to promote partial elemental ordering or phase segregation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to service regimes involving catalytic operations at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion arising from random multi-element mixing, which enhances the cohesive energy and creates a barrier to atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The entropy-driven, random mixing in HEA nanoparticles produces severe lattice distortions that lower atomic mobility (sluggish diffusion), which in turn minimizes the driving force for phase separation, coalescence, or other detrimental structural rearrangements under high thermal stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical thermal treatment, the randomly mixed HEA nanoparticles will exhibit significantly lower atomic diffusion and maintain their disordered, solid-solution structure, whereas the nanoparticles with induced elemental ordering will show increased atomic mobility leading to observable phase segregation or coarsening.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles fabricated using conventional bimetallic or partially segregated alloy synthesis methods where higher atomic diffusion and phase instability are typically observed under similar thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles in the near-equiatomic regime where the size and composition support full entropy stabilization; if nanoparticle dimensions are excessively large or if temperatures exceed the regime where lattice distortion can effectively impede diffusion, other kinetic or thermodynamic factors may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of lattice distortion versus purely thermodynamic mixing effects remains uncertain; additionally, the interaction of the nanoparticles with supports or other environmental factors in real operating conditions may modulate the observed stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of nanoparticles with the same multi-element composition. One batch is produced under rapid synthesis conditions that enforce a high-entropy, randomly mixed state, while the other is post-annealed to promote partial elemental ordering. Subject both batches to thermal cycling in the range of 773–1173 K (mimicking catalytic operation) and characterize the structural evolution using in-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy for elemental mapping.
measurements: Atomic diffusion rates (via in-situ tracer methods or indirect measurement of coarsening rates)
Structural morphology changes (degree of coalescence, phase separation, and particle shape evolution)
Elemental distribution homogeneity before and after thermal treatment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy, randomly mixed nanoparticles do not show a statistically significant reduction in atomic diffusion and better retention of the disordered solid-solution structure compared to the annealed, partially ordered nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion-induced sluggish diffusion governs stability will be falsified.

The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). In an effort to better understand the high robustness of the HEA NPs, theoretical investigations were conducted employing cluster models. DFT calculations demonstrated that the cohesive energy (Ec) of a Co16Ni15Cu16Ru16Pd16 HEA cluster was −3.92 eV, which was higher than the value of −3.09 eV for a Pd79 cluster (Fig. 7a). Combining these data with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, diffusion coefficients (D) were determined at 900 K after 0.1 ps (Supplementary Fig. 18). The results demonstrated that the D values of all metals in a Co16Ni15Cu16Ru16Pd16 HEA cluster were lower than those for the corresponding monometallic clusters (Co79, Cu79, Ni79, Ru79, or Pd79) (Fig. 7b). As an example, the D for Pd in a Co16Ni16Cu15Ru16Pd16 HEA cluster was calculated to be 1.31 × 10−5 m2/s, and so was approximately one-third lower than the value of 3.43 × 10−5 m2/s for a Pd79 cluster. These results provide further evidence that sluggish diffusion in the HEA NPs, originating from the mixing of multiple elements and from lattice distortion effects, contributed significantly to the high resistance of the HEA NPs against the undesired irreversible agglomeration and radiation damage process.
